title: Love Don't Cost a Thing
full_review:
Hoping to look cool to his peers, a nerdy high school senior hires the school's most popular cheerleader to pretend to be his girlfriend in the artless comedy "Love Don't Cost a Thing" (Warner Bros.).

Pretty Paris (Christina Milian) is in big trouble when she damages her mother's car, but classmate Alvin (Nick Cannon) offers to pay for repairs -- provided she's willing to pose around school as his girlfriend for a couple of weeks. No funny business, mind you, but Paris is still turned off at the idea of hanging out with the super-smart but decidedly uncool Alvin. He's really more into his studies than girls, something which drives his oversexed dad (Steve Harvey) crazy.

Once Dad hears Alvin and Paris are apparently a couple, he goes into overdrive, urging his innocent son to leave his virginal status in the dust and become a chip off the old block. Dad goes as far as giving Alvin a hope chest, his "legacy" as he calls it -- filled with condoms. The sight of Dad with a condom is a turn-on to Mom but drives Alvin right out of the house in a panic. Over at Paris' house, her mom is not much of a role model either as she's clueless about whom her daughter dates.
Paris lives her life based on her looks and being cool and gives Alvin a style makeover which goes to his head -- as in swelled head. But she's also touched to learn Alvin used his scholarship money to fix her car. Surprise, surprise, she starts seeing him as a person.

Alvin, meanwhile, is dealing with his dad's pressure on him to become a stud while his uncool friends no longer want to be around conceited Alvin.

Eventually, we know it will all work out with Alvin learning he can just be himself, especially after Dad realizes he was wrong to want a clone of himself for a son instead of valuing Alvin's superior intelligence.

Yet, although the message of co-writer-director Troy Beyer's movie suggests that teens shouldn't give in to peer (or parental) pressure to have sex, the film presents casual sex as very much the norm. The father's change of heart also seems too little, too late, as the film is filled with cheap laughs, without being fresh or funny.

There's a sweet story somewhere buried under all the stereotypical characters, crass gestures and sexual references but with abstinence not even suggested by the parents as a course of action, "Love" doesn't deserve to be embraced.
Due to a parental figure encouraging casual sex and condom usage and crude sexual references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
